name: Democracy
summary: Democracy holds that political authority rests on the people, who rule themselves as political equals, usually by electing representatives in free and periodic elections. Its mainstream, liberal form pairs majority rule with civil liberties, equality before the law and constitutional protection of minorities. It is a view about who should hold power and how, and takes few positions on economic, social or foreign policy.
scope: The mainstream modern ideal of representative, liberal democracy as set out in John Stuart Mill's Considerations on Representative Government, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Article 21) and the Stanford Encyclopedia's account of democratic theory. It treats democracy as a political ideal, not a bundle of economic or cultural policies, so most statements outside government and rights are answered neutral with low confidence. It excludes democratic socialism and social democracy, which have their own profiles.

sources.title: Democracy
sources.author: United Nations
sources.usedFor: The UN account of democracy as a core value embodied in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (the will of the people as the basis of the authority of government)

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The Universal Declaration bars distinctions of birth and status, and Mill defends political equality against rule by inherited rank.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Democratic adherents split between militant-democracy constitutions that bar fascism and neutral ones, and the ideology is silent on it.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Article 18 of the Universal Declaration protects the freedom to change one's religion, which democratic rights frameworks treat as non-negotiable.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Democracy holds that authority rests on the will of the people expressed in elections, not on a self-appointed armed vanguard.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Democrats split between militant democracy, which bans anti-constitutional parties, and the view that free politics must include radicals.

bound-labor.rationale: Democracy presupposes equal citizenship and equal dignity, incompatible with hereditary legal bondage.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Mill holds that the representative assembly's core function is to control the government, including voting taxes and supply; legislative control of the purse is a standard democratic principle.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Mill and the Stanford entry treat elections, parties and organised representation as the means by which citizens rule, so bypassing them contradicts representative democracy.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Mill defended temporary despotism over less advanced peoples while the UDHR affirms self-government for all; the ideal itself is split.

clerical-rule.rationale: The Universal Declaration makes the will of the people the basis of authority, which excludes rule by clergy as such.

collective-bargaining.rationale: The UDHR protects the right to form and join trade unions, but it does not say how wages should be set.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Mill holds that dependencies should be governed for the good of the governed, and the UDHR bases authority on the will of the people, so rule for the metropole's benefit is rejected.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Article 21 says the will of the people is the basis of the authority of government, and Mill grounds legitimate government in the people's consent.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Mainstream liberal democracy pairs majority rule with constitutional protection of minorities, so it does not put majorities above courts and rights.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Equality before the law and the right to privacy (UDHR Articles 2, 7 and 12) tell against criminalising private adult conduct.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Article 25 of the Universal Declaration gives everyone the right to a standard of living adequate for health and well-being, with security in unemployment, sickness and old age.

democracy-best.rationale: Mill argues that even a benevolent despot leaves citizens passive and that self-government is the ideally best form; democrats value popular rule above the quality of any one outcome.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: The mainstream account defines democracy by competitive, free and periodic elections, but the liberal form also requires civil liberties and rule of law, so adherents largely but not fully accept a purely procedural test.

destroy-worshipped-objects.rationale: Article 18 of the Universal Declaration protects freedom of religion, including manifesting it in worship, which destroying what people worship would violate.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Dictatorial power for one class contradicts political equality and equality before the law.

direct-action.rationale: Democracy channels change through free elections, though theorists defend principled civil disobedience as a supplement.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Democrats are split between presidential and parliamentary systems; Mill favoured parliamentary government.

direct-votes.rationale: Direct and representative forms are both democratic and the tradition is divided over which is better.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: The Universal Declaration gives men and women the right to marry without any limitation due to race, nationality or religion, which rules out discouraging it.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: UDHR bars discrimination and promotes equality before the law, but democrats are split on whether discrimination is judged by intent or outcome.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Mill argues sex is irrelevant to political rights and the UDHR bars distinctions of sex.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Article 21 of the UDHR states that the will of the people is the basis of the authority of government, not divine mandate.

divinely-chosen-superior-people.rationale: The Universal Declaration states that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights, without distinction of race or origin, which is incompatible with one people being superior to the rest.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Democracy places authority in the people through free elections among political equals, which is incompatible with office passing by birth.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Liberal democracy pairs majority rule with constitutional protection of rights and the rule of law, so suspending protections is itself a danger.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Liberal democracy pairs majority rule with constitutional protection of rights and minorities.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Declaration states that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights and are equal before the law.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Mill says nationality may rest on shared history or sympathy and none of race, language or religion is strictly required; democratic citizenship is not ethnic.

every-country-ready-for-democracy.rationale: Mill argues that peoples in a savage or wild state, or too passive and submissive to tyranny, are unfit for representative government, so not every country is ready (ch. 4).

experts-over-public.rationale: Expert rule is the classic opposing case (Plato); Mill would have experts draft laws but leaves decision to the elected assembly, and citizens set the aims.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Democracy is tied to equal rights and due process; the Universal Declaration guarantees a fair public trial and presumption of innocence, which killing without trial violates.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Democratic theory is split between the self-determination of peoples and majority rule within existing borders, and gives no settled answer.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: The Stanford entry discusses the boundary problem and the principle that those subject to decisions should have a say, and local residence is a commonly accepted basis; democrats differ.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Mill rejects even benevolent despotism because people ruled at another's discretion lose their agency, and democratic self-rule is justified against arbitrary power.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Equal rights are central to democracy but adherents are split on this specific recognition policy.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: Mill says it is desirable that the chief of the executive hold the power to dissolve Parliament, even where his tenure is fixed, to avoid deadlock between executive and assembly (ch. 18).

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: The UDHR recognises the right to marry and found a family without restriction, which rules out state-steered reproduction.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Political equality means leadership is open to all citizens whatever their ancestry.

indirect-election.rationale: Mill accepts indirect elements while the direct-vote ideal opposes them, and democrats differ on electoral design.

informal-organisation.rationale: Democracy accepts both parties and informal groups as means of association.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: Democratic theory does not settle this; democrats split between sovereignty and international accountability.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Democratic theory holds laws should be justifiable by reasons all citizens can accept.

leader-cult.rationale: Democratic equality and accountability cut against glorifying leaders as embodiments of the nation; Mill warned against concentrating adulation and power in one person.

member-state-blocks-federal-overreach.rationale: Mill holds that disputes over federal powers must go to an independent Supreme Court that is supreme over state and federal governments alike, not to the member states themselves (ch. 17).

military-guardian-role.rationale: Democracy requires civilian control, with authority resting on the people's will (UDHR Art. 21), not an army guardian.

minority-veto.rationale: Majority rule with minority protections is the mainstream view; a veto for each member would let any member block the majority.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Mixed government is an older theory that modern democrats often see as embodied in checks and balances; Mill also favoured representation tempered by safeguards, but adherents are divided.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Democratic theory allows both national constitutional primacy and international rights law; adherents differ.

national-self-determination.rationale: Mill holds that where national feeling is strong people should generally be governed by their own nationality, and self-determination is a leading answer to the boundary problem.

natural-rulers.rationale: Democracy assumes the political equality of citizens and equality before the law, and rejects fixed ruling classes.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Liberal democracy generally favours secular citizenship, yet consociational democracies share power by religious community, so adherents are split.

office-by-exam.rationale: Mill favours competitive examination for administrative posts but insists the governing body be elected, so a democrat generally rejects exams in place of election for political office.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: The mainstream ideal selects officials by free, periodic elections (UDHR Article 21; Mill), though the Stanford entry notes lotteries as an Athenian democratic tool.

one-party-rule.rationale: Authority is to rest on genuine periodic elections, and narrow definitions of democracy require competitive elections between rulers.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Mill values citizens' active public participation in local and public functions, and the Stanford entry discusses participatory forms, though representative democrats stress delegation.

party-controls-media.rationale: The UDHR protects freedom of opinion and expression, and democratic theory requires independent information to hold rulers to account.

political-decisions-consensus.rationale: The Stanford entry notes that requiring consensus or unanimity fails because there is rarely agreement, and that decision procedures exist to settle matters despite disagreement; the democratic rule is not unanimity.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Mill favoured federation for peoples that suit it, but democracy as such does not decide whether nations should pool sovereignty.

population-transfer.rationale: Liberal democracy rests on equal rights and protection of minorities, and the Declaration bars arbitrary exile and guarantees nationality and the right to leave and return.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Democrats differ between majority rule and consociational power-sharing; the sources treat both as democratic.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Democrats value press freedom and political equality but split on whether wealth undermines them, so adherents are divided.

property-franchise.rationale: Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights calls for universal and equal suffrage, which rules out property or tax qualifications.

proportional-representation.rationale: Mill calls proportional representation of minorities the mark of true democracy, though democrats differ on electoral systems.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Informed citizens and free expression require access to public information; the UDHR protects seeking and receiving information.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The UDHR guarantees freedom of thought, conscience and religion (Article 18), which punishing blasphemy or false worship would violate.

racial-franchise.rationale: Universal and equal suffrage under the UDHR bars restricting political rights to one racial or ethnic group.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Equality before the law and non-discrimination by race are foundational to democratic citizenship.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Liberal democracy protects freedom of religion and equality before the law, which the UDHR Article 18 frames as equal freedom for all beliefs, though democracies differ on established churches.

remove-indigenous-peoples.rationale: The Universal Declaration bars arbitrary exile and distinctions of race or origin, and guarantees equal rights to everyone, which excludes removing a people from its lands.

remove-other-ethnic-groups-from-country.rationale: The Universal Declaration bars arbitrary exile and distinctions of race or origin, and protects the right to a nationality, which excludes expelling an ethnic group.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Article 18 of the Declaration includes the freedom to change one's religion or belief, so legal restriction is excluded.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Mill and the UDHR treat free expression, association and electoral rights as essential, so suspending them cannot be justified by growth.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Democracies differ on whether free expression may be limited to protect minorities; there is no common democratic position.

right-to-secede.rationale: The boundary problem is unsettled in democratic theory; some tie borders to self-determination, others keep existing borders.

sacred-nation.rationale: Mill treats nationality as a practical condition for government, not a sacred matter; adherents differ.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Democracy holds that authority comes from the people, not from divine descent; the UDHR says the will of the people is the basis of government.

separated-powers.rationale: Liberal democracy pairs majority rule with constitutional limits, and Mill defends checks on representative bodies and majorities.

single-common-good.rationale: Democratic theory includes both Rousseau's general will and models that balance competing interests; adherents differ.

single-official-language.rationale: Mill thought free institutions work best within one nationality, but liberal democracies also protect minority language rights; democrats are split.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Mill discusses nationality and federation as practical matters, and democrats differ on whether borders follow peoples.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Constitutional democracy requires rulers to be bound by law and accountable; the UDHR rests human rights on the rule of law.

state-harmful.rationale: Democracy is a form of government through which a people rules itself, so it presupposes a state worth controlling.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Liberal democracy protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion (UDHR Article 18), which rules out state promotion of atheism.

strong-leader.rationale: Democracy rests on rule of law, constitutional limits and citizen participation, and Mill warns that rule by one capable person breeds passive citizens.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The UDHR protects freedom of association and assembly (Article 20) and makes free, periodic elections the basis of authority (Article 21); suppressing opposition negates this.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Mill calls conquest that subjugates a people a serious harm and regards free institutions as resting on self-government.

torture-always-illegal.rationale: Article 5 of the Universal Declaration states that no one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

total-state.rationale: Democracy is tied to civil liberties and rights of expression, association and conscience which a state directing all life would remove.

unions-good.rationale: The UDHR protects the right to form unions and association is a democratic freedom, though democracy as such does not rank their social value.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Democrats split: some say voters should decide, others say term limits guard against entrenchment.

voter-id.rationale: Democrats agree on free and fair elections but split between protecting ballot integrity and avoiding barriers to voting, so it is left neutral.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: The Universal Declaration gives men and women equal rights as to marriage and at its dissolution, which supports a wife's ability to divorce without the husband's consent.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Mill and democratic theory treat active citizenship as valuable and as a safeguard of self-rule.

women-must-cover.rationale: The Universal Declaration protects equality, religion and expression as personal freedoms, which a legal dress mandate for women contradicts.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Political and legal equality is central to democracy, and the Universal Declaration affirms equal rights and the right to own property without distinction of sex.

women-suffrage.rationale: Political equality is central to democracy; Mill argued for women's suffrage and the UDHR (Article 21) guarantees everyone the right to take part in government.

missingStatements.text: Legislative seats should be allocated to parties in proportion to the votes they receive.
missingStatements.rationale: Mill argues that true democracy represents minorities in proportion to their numbers, and the Stanford entry compares proportional with single-member systems, though democrats differ on the electoral system.

notes: Democracy is treated as a political method. Democratic socialists, liberals and populists who call themselves democrats answer many economic and social statements differently, which is why most of those answers are neutral and low confidence.
